line: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 Bb5+ Bd7 Be2 Nxd5 d4 Bf5
teaches: Counting development means counting MOVES, not pieces — a piece that reaches its good square on the second try has cost two moves and delivered one developed piece, and that arithmetic is the whole reason a side stands slightly better out of a quiet opening. When you must move a piece twice, make the second square earn it.
explains: The bishop leaves the square the check pushed it to and comes to f5, where it does hit the pawn on c2 and cover the central light squares. It is a good square — reached one move late.

line: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 Bb5+ Bd7 Be2 Nxd5 d4 Bf5 Nf3 e6 c4 Nb4
teaches: A pawn move that gains space also stops guarding the squares it has left behind — before playing the natural expanding move, look at which square in your own camp becomes permanently unavailable to your pawns, because a knight that lands there cannot be chased and cannot be ignored either.
explains: The advance takes the centre but abandons d3, and the knight drops in on b4 eyeing that square and c2 while hitting the pawn on a2. There is no pawn left that can ever ask it to move.
